name: Straight leg jeans

lead: Straight leg jeans have about the same width at the leg opening as at the thigh-to-hem line. Clothing guides and forum posters suggest the cut flatters many body types.
The appearance payoff is proportion: a straight line from knee to hem avoids both the skin-tight look of skinny jeans and the sagging look of loose fits.

paras: People wear them in darker washes and with a fit that sits at the natural waist, hemmed at the shoe.
Few risks; fit varies by brand and by thigh and calf size.

angle.text: The cut is chosen for how it frames the legs without clinging or sagging. Users say it suits a range of builds.

lead: Straight leg jeans are a denim cut in which the leg opening is roughly as wide as the leg above it, giving a fit that is slightly relaxed rather than tapered.[1] The jeans themselves date to riveted work trousers patented by Jacob Davis and Levi Strauss in 1873.[1]

On T Nation fashion threads, a poster suggested straight-cut or boot-cut jeans because they taper down and avoid a saggy look from behind, while another said straight and boot cuts "tend to look great on everyone".[2][3]

paras: Wikipedia describes straight-leg as roughly the same width at the opening as at the leg, in contrast to slim, skinny and flared cuts.[1] High-waisted styles popular in the 1970s have returned, and low rise cycled in the 1990s to 2000s and again in the 2020s.[1]
Fashion advice threads point to dark washes and straight or boot cuts as safe choices.[2][3]

timeline.event: Davis and Strauss patent riveted work trousers.[1]
Levi's introduces pre-shrunk jeans, including the 505 regular fit.[1]
